questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a restoration decision must rest on
questions.stem: An entry in the dispatcher's log records a decision to remove a darkened varnish from the panel in the station waiting room, and asks what that decision must rest on.

options.text: That the layer is a later addition and that removing it will not disturb the original paint beneath.
That visitors find the panel dull and prefer the brighter look a fresh surface gives.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: That the panel is old and therefore too fragile to be cleaned by anyone at all.
options.misconception: reads wear as evidence of age

options.text: That a restorer in another city has cleaned a similar panel in the same way.
options.misconception: assumes one restorer's work settles another's

questions.explanation: The decision must rest on what the layer is and on what removal would carry away. Preference and the age of the panel are not evidence, and another restorer's practice settles nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the layer is and what it is hiding.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a feature-by-feature comparison
questions.stem: A second entry in the same log compares a suspect copy with the panel it claims to copy, listing nine recorded features of which seven match and two do not.

options.text: The copy is a close one, and the two mismatched features are where the investigation should start.
The copy is proved false, since a copy that matches seven features cannot be by the same hand.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: The copy is proved genuine, since a false version would have failed on all nine features.
options.misconception: believes a signature proves the hand

options.text: The two features that differ cannot be evidence, since a copy was never expected to agree.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

questions.explanation: A copy matching most features but not all is what careful imitation looks like, and the mismatches are where the argument lies. Neither agreement nor difference alone settles the case.
questions.hint: Look at which features disagree, not at the count.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sequence of scenes carries meaning
questions.stem: The log asks why the portal of a parish church carries its scenes in that order, and the archivist answers in a short statement for the file.

answer.exemplar: The order of the scenes is itself part of the message, because a viewer who knows the sequence reads the carvings as a story rather than as a set of figures. The position of each scene tells the visitor what has happened before and what is expected to follow, and the placing of the largest figures marks the moments that mattered most to the church.

questions.explanation: A sequence tells a visitor what comes before and after, and it marks the scenes that carried the most weight. Reading the portal as unrelated figures loses the argument built into the order.
questions.hint: Read the portal as a sequence, not as figures.

questions.stem: A charter of 1189 in the station archive records a gift of forty wax candles a year to a shrine, and a monastic note says the delivery was doubled in 1197. How many candles were delivered in 1197?
questions.explanation: The charter sets the yearly gift at forty candles, and the note says the delivery was doubled in 1197. Doubling forty gives eighty candles for that year, and the note is a later addition.
questions.hint: Double the yearly figure the charter records.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a still life was shaped for its market

stimulus.body: The refreshment room still life shows a table with a peeled lemon, a bread roll, a wine glass, a knife and a loaf of bread, with a shelf of jars and a basket of figs behind. The entry notes that the picture was bought by the company for the station buffet in 1908.

questions.stem: A log entry sets down a still life hanging in the station refreshment room, and the archivist is asked how the picture was shaped for the market it was bought for.

options.text: The full shelf and the cut lemon present goods as plenty, which is what a buyer was asked to see.
The knife and the glass show that the picture records one household's meal on one evening.
options.misconception: treats a market picture as a private record

options.text: The still life was painted for a private collector, since such pictures were never bought for public rooms.
options.misconception: believes such pictures were never made for sale

options.text: The arrangement shows the artist's skill in still life, which was the reason the company bought the picture.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

questions.explanation: A picture made for sale carries the qualities buyers looked for, and a buffet buyer wanted abundance and appetite. The scene shows goods rather than recording an evening, and that is the point of it.
questions.hint: Ask what a buyer of food was expected to see.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: Read a provenance line without adding to it
questions.stem: One line of the provenance is copied into the log, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to separate what the line states from what it infers, and then to say what it proves.

options.text: Separate stated owners from implied gaps, then say the line documents only what it names.
Treat the earliest name as the original owner, then accept that the picture never left the region.
options.misconception: takes the oldest record as the truest

options.text: Treat the longest string of owners as proof of importance, then value the picture accordingly.
options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

options.text: Treat a gap in the line as a theft, then report the missing years to the company.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

questions.explanation: A provenance line states what a document records and leaves the rest unsaid, and those silences are where readers supply too much. The line documents the owners it names and no others.
questions.hint: Separate the owners named from the years implied.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Write a comparison label that describes rather than ranks
questions.stem: A request in the log asks for wording that describes two works shown side by side, and the archivist drafts a sentence about the older work that calls it crude by comparison.

options.text: The sentence states a verdict rather than a difference, and a comparison should describe both treatments.
The sentence is fair, since a visible difference in handling is a fact that visitors can see.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: The sentence is unfair only because it names the older work, so naming the newer one would settle it.
options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

options.text: The sentence cannot be judged, since words about handling are always a matter of opinion.
options.misconception: treats wording about handling as pure opinion

questions.explanation: Calling a work crude is a verdict on worth, and a comparison label should set out how two treatments differ. A visible difference in handling is a fact, and describing it does not rank the works.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sentence describes or ranks.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a cleaning test and its limits
questions.stem: A test-cleaning record in the log notes three small areas swabbed, and that two lifted a dark layer while the third left a dull film that no solvent moved.

options.text: The test shows two surfaces are removable and one is original, so the plan must be limited to the two.
The test shows the whole panel is safe to clean, since a solvent that moved one layer will move them all.
options.misconception: assumes one sample settles the whole surface

options.text: The test proves the dull film is a later varnish, since nothing moved it and later coatings resist solvents.
options.misconception: assumes a material that resists is therefore later

options.text: The test shows the panel is a later copy, since a genuine painting resists solvents better than a false one.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

questions.explanation: A test on small areas shows what can be moved at those points, and the result differs across the surface, so the plan must be selective. One swab says nothing about the whole panel.
questions.hint: Read the test as local evidence, not a blanket verdict.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: State what a forgery has to match
questions.stem: The log asks what a convincing copy must match, and the archivist answers in a short statement for the file.

answer.exemplar: A false version has to match the original in the features a viewer will actually notice, which for a devotional picture means the composition, the faces and the principal colours, and it has to reproduce the scale and the setting of the original closely enough to pass as it. What it does not have to match is the handling of the brush, the wear of the surface, and the small material traces that the passage of centuries leaves behind.

questions.explanation: A copy succeeds by matching what the eye checks first, and fails where the hand is more exacting. Handling, wear and material traces separate a close imitation from the original.
questions.hint: Ask which features a viewer's eye checks first.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference in counts from a portal record
questions.stem: A church portal in the region carries twelve carved figures on the left jamb and eighteen on the right, and the log asks how many more figures the right jamb carries than the left.
questions.explanation: The right jamb carries eighteen figures and the left twelve, so the difference is 18 minus 12. That gives 6, the extra figures on the right jamb, before any account of the lintel.
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller count from the larger.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A charter, a saint, and a gift
questions.learningObjective: Explain how documents and objects build a record

stimulus.body: A charter of 1120 records a gift of a brooch to a shrine of a local saint. A later note in the same hand says the shrine was visited each year on the saint's day, and that a list of gifts was kept beside the altar.

questions.stem: A station note records a charter, a saint and a gift, and the archivist is asked what the three together establish about the shrine.

options.text: That a document and a devotional object built the same record of the shrine, each supporting the other.
That the brooch was stolen, since a gift recorded in a charter must be a loss recorded later.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

options.text: That the saint was invented later, since a shrine with gifts must be a story made up after the charter.
options.misconception: treats a gift as proof that the saint was invented

options.text: That the list of gifts was the charter, since both record the same offering in the same year.
options.misconception: confuses a document with a monument

questions.explanation: A charter fixes a gift in law and a shrine list records the cult around it, so the two show an institution and an object sustaining each other. Neither suggests a theft.
questions.hint: Ask what a charter and a shrine list each record.

questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Read a still life for the market it was made for
questions.stem: A log entry records a still life that was bought for the station buffet, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to say what the picture offers the buyer, and then to say what it claims about the goods.

options.text: Show what the picture offers as plenty, then show it as goods with a value the buyer can recognise.
Show the household that owned the fruit, then show the food as the record of a single meal.
options.misconception: treats a market picture as a private record

options.text: Show the painter's skill in still life, then show the arrangement as the only subject worth painting.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

options.text: Show that the goods were imported, then show the market as the reason the picture was bought.
options.misconception: reads a subject as the maker's belief

questions.explanation: A still life for sale leads with what the buyer wants, which is abundance, and makes the goods legible as goods. Reading it as a household record ignores the bargain the picture was made for.
questions.hint: Ask what a buyer was expected to take from it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: State what a sale record establishes
questions.stem: The log copies out an ownership line from a nineteenth-century sale, and the archivist asks what the line does and does not establish.

options.text: It records the owners named at that sale and leaves the earlier history of the work unstated.
It proves the work was never in another country, since a sale records where a picture stayed.
options.misconception: takes a sale catalogue as a complete history

options.text: It proves the work was painted for the buyer named in it, since such sales listed new pictures only.
options.misconception: assumes a document describes the making of a work

options.text: It proves the work is the original and not a copy, since a copy would have been sold separately.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

questions.explanation: A sale line is a record of a transaction at one moment, and it says nothing about where the work was before or how it was made. Treat it as a stage in a history rather than as the whole history.
questions.hint: A sale line records one moment, not the whole story.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Identify the judgement inside a drafted label
questions.stem: Two labels have been drafted to describe the same pair of works, and the log counts the differences: the first mentions colour, scale and date, the second adds the painter's reputation and calls one work a period piece.

options.text: The second label adds a judgement the comparison cannot support, since reputation is not a feature.
The second label is fuller, and a longer label always helps a visitor understand two works.
options.misconception: assumes longer is always better

options.text: The first label is too short, since a comparison needs at least four features to be worth reading.
options.misconception: counts features instead of choosing them

options.text: Both labels are wrong, since a comparison should never mention the date of the works at all.
options.misconception: ignores what the paint layer can show

questions.explanation: A comparison label should name features that can be looked at, and a painter's reputation is a fact about the art world, not about the paint. The second label adds a verdict.
questions.hint: Ask whether each phrase names a visible feature.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a restoration decision is documented
questions.stem: The dispatcher's log asks the archivist to explain in a short statement why a decision to restore has to be written down with the reasoning attached.

answer.exemplar: A treatment is irreversible in practice, and a written record of what was done and why is the only way a later curator can judge whether the work was improved or diminished. The record also shows what was left untouched, so that a future decision can build on the last one instead of repeating it, and it protects the institution from a second generation of guessing.

questions.explanation: Treatment changes the object, and a later curator can only judge it if the reasoning was written down at the time. Recording it also lets a second decision build on the first instead of repeating it.
questions.hint: Ask what a later curator would need in order to judge.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: Read a portal sequence and its limits

stimulus.body: The west portal of a parish church carries a carved panel of the Last Supper at the centre, with panels of washing and betrayal on the left and a panel of a woman at an empty tomb on the right. The parish note records that the masons' accounts list the panels in that order from left to right.

questions.stem: A note from the parish describes the sculpted panels on a west portal, and the archivist is asked what the note allows the reader to claim about the sequence.

options.text: That the panels were carved in a deliberate order, and that a visitor could read them as a sequence of events.
That the centre panel was the first to be carved, since the most important subject is always made first.
options.misconception: assumes importance decides the order of work

options.text: That the masons chose the subjects, since the accounts list what they made rather than what was wanted.
options.misconception: assumes a document records the choices of one person

options.text: That the portal was rebuilt in the order of the accounts, since medieval craftsmen never altered a plan.
options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

questions.explanation: An account listing the panels in order shows that the order was fixed, and a visitor who knows the sequence reads the portal as a story. It does not tell us who chose the subjects.
questions.hint: Ask what a listed order can and cannot fix.

questions.learningObjective: Combine a charter and a shrine list without merging them
questions.stem: A log entry about a relic records both a gift of money to a shrine and a list of pilgrims' names, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to say what the documents establish, and then to say what the two together suggest.

options.text: Establish the gift and the names, then suggest that the shrine's importance grew over time.
Establish the gift and the names, then conclude that the gift bought the shrine its right to the relic.
options.misconception: treats a payment as proof of ownership rights

options.text: Establish the gift and the names, then conclude that the pilgrims listed were the donors of the money.
options.misconception: reads two lists as one

options.text: Establish the gift and the names, then conclude that the shrine was founded in the year of the gift.
options.misconception: takes the oldest record as the truest

questions.explanation: A payment and a list of names are separate records, one about money and one about visitors. Read together they suggest a shrine whose importance grew, not a single founding event.
questions.hint: Keep the two documents apart before combining them.

questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of details in a sale picture
questions.stem: The log describes a still life that was made to sell, with a half-eaten pie and a tipped wine glass, and asks what the painter is doing with those details.

options.text: The broken and finished things suggest that the meal is passing, which shows what is worth having.
The painter is recording a banquet that took place, since every detail in the picture was witnessed.
options.misconception: treats a market picture as a private record

options.text: The painter is copying another picture, since the tipped glass appears in several known works.
options.misconception: assumes a repeated motif proves a copy

options.text: The painter is warning against gluttony, since spoiled food was a common moral in such pictures.
options.misconception: reads a subject as the maker's belief

questions.explanation: Half-eaten food and a tipped glass make the scene look caught in the act, which shows goods as worth having now. Such pictures were made to sell, and the details serve the bargain.
questions.hint: Ask what the details do for the buyer.

questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to read an incomplete ownership line
questions.stem: A single ownership line in the log records a sale in 1668 with no other information, and the archivist must explain how such a line should be read.

answer.exemplar: A line that gives a name, a place and a year is a witness to one transaction and to nothing more, and the years before it are simply unknown rather than settled. A careful reader marks the gap in the record instead of filling it with a guess about where the work came from, and says plainly that the earlier history has not been traced.

questions.explanation: A single dated line is a witness to one transaction, and the years before it are unknown rather than settled. The careful course is to mark the gap instead of filling it with a guess.
questions.hint: A gap in a record is a gap, not a fact.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a restoration request is tested against

stimulus.body: A restoration request asks for the yellowed varnish on a panel in the station waiting room to be removed and the panel to be revarnished. The request adds that the last inspection, made in 1974, recorded the varnish as stable and the paint as sound beneath it.

questions.stem: A restoration request in the log asks for a treatment, and the archivist is asked what the request must be tested against before it is agreed.

options.text: The state of the paint beneath, since removing the varnish can only be judged by what lies under it.
The date of the last inspection, since a treatment more than fifty years old is always out of date.
options.misconception: judges currency by age alone

options.text: The wishes of the company, since a request from the owner of the room settles the treatment.
options.misconception: assumes a request settles the case

options.text: The cost of the work, since a cheaper treatment is the one the station can afford.
options.misconception: judges a treatment by price

questions.explanation: A treatment must be tested against the object it touches, and the paint beneath the varnish is what is at risk. Age of report, company wishes and cost matter less than that.
questions.hint: Ask what the treatment will actually touch.

options.misconception: believes a value equals a judgement of art

questions.stem: The refreshment room still life is described in the log, and the archivist must explain how a picture made for the market used its subject to sell.

answer.exemplar: A picture made for sale is built out of the things a buyer expects to find in the picture, and the artist arranges them so the eye moves from one to the next through a rhythm of highlights, textures and decay. questions.explanation: A picture made for sale is built from what a buyer expects, and the subject is the argument of the bargain. The handling serves the showing of goods, and reading it as a private record misreads it.

questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Judge comparative wording after a rewrite

stimulus.body: A comparison label for two works reads: the earlier panel sets the figures against a plain ground and gives the hands more room, while the later panel crowds the table edge to the frame and handles the fruit with a sharper touch. options.text: That a comparison label can describe handling in detail and still avoid ranking the two works.
That handling cannot be described at all, since every descriptive word carries a judgement.
options.misconception: treats all description as judgement

options.text: That the two works should not be shown together, since their handling is so different.
options.misconception: assumes a display must be decided by taste

options.text: That the later panel is the better painting, since the word removed was accurate in the first place.
options.misconception: reads a difference of date as a ranking

questions.explanation: A comparison label can describe brushwork closely without ranking the works, and the rewrite shows a curator tightening words. One removed word does not make a contest of the pair.
questions.hint: Ask whether the revised words still rank the works.

questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Decide a treatment in two stages of reasoning
questions.stem: The log asks the archivist to decide, in two stages, whether to treat a station panel: first to state what a treatment would do, and then to state what evidence would justify it.

options.text: State what the treatment would remove, then set the evidence the decision must rest on.
State what the treatment would remove, then treat the officer's approval as the evidence needed.
options.misconception: assumes a request settles the case

options.text: State what the treatment would remove, then choose the treatment that is cheapest to carry out.
options.misconception: judges a treatment by price

options.text: State what the treatment would remove, then leave the panel alone, since doing nothing needs no evidence.
options.misconception: treats inaction as a decision without evidence

questions.explanation: The first stage describes what a treatment would do, and the second names the evidence that would make it acceptable. Approval is not evidence, and inaction is a decision.
questions.hint: Ask what the treatment does and what justifies it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: Read a surface difference as evidence
questions.stem: A canvas offered for the station collection matches a documented work in composition and in size, but the paint surface is sound and uncracked, and the log asks what that means.

options.text: That the surface is younger than the composition it copies, so the two cannot be the same object.
That the canvas is an excellent copy, since a sound surface is a mark of careful work.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: That the copy must be recent, since only modern makers can copy a composition exactly.
options.misconception: assumes only modern makers can copy well

options.text: That the surface tells us nothing, since cracking depends on where a picture is hung.
options.misconception: dismisses surface evidence as irrelevant

questions.explanation: A surface with no cracking has not been through the centuries the copied composition has, so the two are separate objects. A careful copy is possible, and sound paint is a plain way of telling.
questions.hint: Ask how long each surface has been in existence.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a sequence of scenes communicates
questions.stem: The log asks what the sequence of scenes on a portal tells a visitor, and the archivist answers in a short statement for the file.

answer.exemplar: A visitor who knows the order of the scenes reads the portal as a narrative rather than as a wall of carved figures, and the order decides how much of each subject is understood before the next one is seen. The carver therefore places the scenes so that the story advances, and reserves the largest and highest position for the moment the church most wanted a visitor to remember.

questions.explanation: Sequence turns a wall of figures into a story the visitor can follow, and it sets the emphasis by position. The programme is an argument about what matters, addressed to people expected to read.
questions.hint: Ask what a visitor gains from the order.

questions.hint: Subtract the earlier year from the later one.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Identify the details that sell a still life

stimulus.body: A still life entered in the log shows a silver dish of oysters, a lemon with its peel spiralling down the table edge, a roemer glass half full, a pewter plate, and a cloth slipping from the table. The entry notes the picture was sold at a fair in the same year the station buffet opened.

questions.stem: A log entry sketches a still life entered for the station buffet, and the archivist is asked which details in the picture work hardest on the buyer.

options.text: The shells, the peel and the slipping cloth, which put movement into a display of goods just served.
The silver and the pewter, since the buyer was choosing between sets of plate rather than a picture.
options.misconception: reads a still life as a list of purchases

options.text: The roemer glass, since a half-filled glass is the only element that records a specific evening.
options.misconception: treats a market picture as a private record

options.text: The oyster dish, since a buyer in 1908 would have been unwilling to look at a picture without one.
options.misconception: judges a picture by its subject alone

questions.explanation: The dropped peel and slipping cloth make the arrangement look caught in movement, which is how a picture of goods suggests they are fresh and ready. The silver shows wealth on offer.
questions.hint: Ask which details suggest movement and freshness.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: Read gaps in an ownership record
questions.stem: An ownership line in the log names four owners, but the gaps between them are 12 years, 30 years and 9 years, and the log asks what the uneven gaps allow a reader to claim.

options.text: That the work is documented unevenly, and that the long gap is where the evidence is thinnest.
That the work changed hands twice only, since long gaps are usually one transfer recorded twice.
options.misconception: reads gaps as lost transactions

options.text: That the long gap marks a period of theft, since that is the usual reason for a gap in a record.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

options.text: That the four owners were the only owners, since a gap of any length must mean no sale took place.
options.misconception: assumes silence proves the absence of events

questions.explanation: Uneven gaps show that the evidence is uneven, and the long gap is where a story is thinnest and most likely to be invented. A gap limits claims, it is not a fact.
questions.hint: Ask where the record is thinnest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a comparison caption should do
questions.stem: The log asks for caption wording that sets two works side by side, and the archivist drafts a short statement in the file.

answer.exemplar: A caption that sets two works together should name the features on which they are being compared, state plainly what is different, and say nothing about which is better, because a visitor is being invited to look rather than to vote. The wording can be exact and still leave the judgement to the person in front of the work, and that is the difference between a comparison and a contest.

questions.explanation: A comparison caption names the features compared, states the differences and stops there. Leaving the judgement to the visitor is not vagueness, it is the difference between comparison and contest.
questions.hint: Name the features and stop before the verdict.

questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Set out a sensible response to flaking paint
questions.stem: A painting in the waiting room is reported to have flaking paint, and the log asks what the station should do about it.

options.text: Record the condition, find out what is causing the flaking, and treat it only as far as that cause allows.
Have the picture varnished at once, since a fresh coat will hold the flaking paint in place.
options.misconception: assumes a coat fixes the cause

options.text: Remove the painting from public view, since a work that is flaking cannot be shown to anyone.
options.misconception: assumes removal is always the answer

options.text: Wait and watch, since flaking often settles by itself once the weather turns warmer.
options.misconception: assumes damage repairs itself

questions.explanation: Flaking is a symptom, and the cause must be found before a treatment is chosen, because a varnish over damp paint fixes nothing. The condition should be recorded and the treatment limited.
questions.hint: Find the cause before choosing the treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret an artificial crack pattern
questions.stem: A log entry notes that a suspected copy of a panel shows a craquelure pattern of uniform size across the whole surface, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to say what that suggests, and then to say what else must be checked.

options.text: Suggest a deliberately applied pattern, then check the support, materials and handling for other signs.
Suggest the work is a photograph, then check the frame for a dealer mark.
options.misconception: treats a pattern as proof of one medium

options.text: Suggest the panel was stored in a very dry room, then check the invoice for the year of purchase.
options.misconception: reads a surface pattern as a storage record

options.text: Suggest the work is genuine, since old panels crack evenly as they dry out with age.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

questions.explanation: An even craquelure of uniform size is a hallmark of a deliberately applied pattern. The other checks are still needed, since the pattern alone names no hand.
questions.hint: Ask what a uniform crack size means.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A charter, a saint, and a gift
questions.learningObjective: Combine charter and later records into one history

stimulus.body: A note in the log quotes a charter of 1156 that records a gift of land to a shrine, and adds that a second charter of 1180 records a bell hung in the same shrine. A marginal note of 1194 says the bell was recast after it cracked.

questions.stem: A note in the log quotes a charter and two later entries about a shrine, and the archivist is asked how the three records work together.

options.text: They build a history in layers, as a gift of land, a later bell and a repair of that bell each belong.
They contradict each other, since a bell that was recast in 1194 cannot have been given in 1180.
options.misconception: assumes one record contradicts another

options.text: They show the shrine was destroyed in 1156 and rebuilt in 1180, which is the only possible reading.
options.misconception: reads silence in a record as denial

options.text: They show the charter is a copy, since a genuine charter would not mention a bell twice.
options.misconception: assumes a repeated detail proves a copy

questions.explanation: The three entries belong to one continuing history, each adding a layer rather than contradicting the others. A bell can be recast and still be the bell that was given.
questions.hint: Ask whether the entries add up or conflict.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Read a still life's subject and its market
questions.stem: A still life in the refreshment room is entered in the log, and the archivist is asked to work in two stages: first to say what the subject offers, and then to say who the picture was made for.

options.text: Say that the subject offers abundance, then say that the picture was made for a buyer in the market.
Say that the subject offers abundance, then say that the picture was made for one household's table.
options.misconception: treats a market picture as a private record

options.text: Say that the subject offers a moral lesson, then say that the picture was made to instruct a child.
options.misconception: reads a subject as the maker's belief

options.text: Say that the subject offers a record of prices, then say that the picture was made to list market rates.
options.misconception: assumes a still life is a document of prices

questions.explanation: A still life of food and vessels offers abundance, and the picture is made for the market because that is the bargain it carries. A household picture or a price list is not what it is.
questions.hint: Ask what the subject offers and who paid for it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a thin provenance line records
questions.stem: The log copies a provenance line that reads: from the collection of a Venetian family, sold at Venice, acquired at Venice, and thence in England. The archivist asks what the line shows.

options.text: That the ownership history is recorded in general terms, with places named but no owners and no dates.
That the picture was painted in Venice, since a picture cannot be made where it never was.
options.misconception: assumes a place of ownership fixes a place of making

options.text: That the picture is a copy, since a work that changes hands so often cannot be original.
options.misconception: assumes a good copy is a bad fake

options.text: That the picture is in its original setting, since the line shows it stayed with one family.
options.misconception: reads a place name as a fixed home

questions.explanation: A line that names places and transfers without owners or dates is a thin record, and it documents movement rather than continuity. It says nothing about where the work was made or what it is.
questions.hint: Notice what the line never names.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Plan a caption for two works of one workshop
questions.stem: Two works from the same workshop are to be shown together, and the archivist must explain how the caption should be written.

answer.exemplar: A caption comparing two works from one workshop should say what the two share, which is the training and the habits they inherited, and what separates them, which is the task and the moment each was painted for. The reader should leave the caption with a sharper sense of two individual hands inside a shared practice, which is a different thing from being told which of them is better.

questions.explanation: A caption for two works from one workshop should state what they share and what separates them, so the reader sees two hands inside a shared practice. Deciding which is better does not belong here.
questions.hint: Say what they share and what separates them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Say what a damage report must record
questions.stem: A second report in the log describes a panel whose paint is lifting in a strip along a join, and asks what the report should record beyond the damage itself.

options.text: The cause, the extent and the treatment already done, so the next decision builds on this one.
The value of the panel, since the damage changes what the insurance will pay for the work.
options.misconception: judges a treatment by price

options.text: The name of the painter, since the join pattern identifies the hand that made the panel.
options.misconception: takes a material as proof of the maker

options.text: The date of the last repair, since nothing else about the panel is any use to a curator.
options.misconception: ignores the damage and its cause

questions.explanation: A damage report is useful for what it enables next, so the cause, the extent and any earlier treatment are the entries that matter. Value and attribution are recorded elsewhere.
questions.hint: Ask what the next decision will need to know.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the evidence in a claim of copying

stimulus.body: An entry describes a painting offered to the station collection as a copy of a well-known panel. The work has the same composition and the same size, but the wood is a different species from the original, the ground contains a synthetic binder, and the pigments match a nineteenth-century maker's catalogue.

questions.stem: A log entry sets out a painting offered as a copy, and the archivist is asked which of the three observations in the entry tells the most.

options.text: The wood, since a support of a different species shows the panel was never the original panel.
The binder, since a synthetic binder in the ground settles the question on its own.
options.misconception: assumes one material settles a case

options.text: The pigments, since matching a catalogue of nineteenth-century makers dates the work precisely.
options.misconception: assumes a pigment catalogue dates a work exactly

options.text: The composition, since a matching composition settles the question of what the work is.
options.misconception: assumes a matching composition proves identity

questions.explanation: A support of a different species cannot be the original panel, so the wood tells most, with the binder and pigments supporting it. None of the three dates the work, and composition settles nothing.
questions.hint: Ask which observation cannot be explained away.

That the other three panels were carved later, since they were not entered in the accounts.

options.misconception: assumes a missing record means a missing panel

options.misconception: assumes payment follows importance

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a span from a dated gift list
questions.stem: A gift list in the archive records three gifts of the same relic, in 1204, 1209 and 1214, and the log asks how many years separate the first and the last.

options.text: Ten years, because the list runs from 1204 to 1214 and the difference is ten.
Fifteen years, because three gifts are spaced at five-year intervals in the list.
options.misconception: assumes an even spacing of recorded events

options.misconception: doubles the record to reach a date

options.misconception: denies a dated record any dating power

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A still life made to sell
questions.learningObjective: Explain the care given to surfaces in a sale picture
questions.stem: A still life from the refreshment room is entered in the log, and the archivist must explain why such pictures were made with so much care about surfaces.

answer.exemplar: In a picture made for sale, the surfaces are the argument. A viewer who cannot tell silver from pewter, or a polished grape from a dull one, has been given nothing to buy, so the artist spends the care on the difficulty of textures rather than on the richness of the subject, and the picture promises the buyer that what is shown can be judged by eye.

questions.explanation: In a picture made for sale, surfaces carry the argument, because a buyer has to be able to read the goods. The care spent on texture turns the picture into a promise about value.
questions.hint: Ask what a buyer has to be able to see.

State the owners and dates as written, then conclude that the work passed directly between them.

options.text: State the owners and dates as written, then conclude that the earliest owner bought the work new.
options.misconception: assumes the earliest owner bought the work new

options.misconception: assumes a documented history is a settled one

questions.explanation: The first stage transcribes what the document says, and the second keeps the conclusion inside it. A chain of names shows a chain of names, and nothing more follows.
questions.hint: Read the line before drawing from it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: Set out what a copy must reproduce
questions.stem: A painting offered to the collection is entered in the log, and the archivist must explain in a short statement what a copy has to reproduce.

answer.exemplar: A copy has to reproduce the original closely enough to pass for it in the setting where the original is known, which means the composition, the figures, the scale and the principal colours, and it has to do so at a size that fits the frame it will hang in. What it does not have to reproduce is the wear, the small losses and the irregularities of a surface that has been handled for three hundred years, and those are usually where the imitation fails.

questions.explanation: A copy has to match what the eye checks first and what the frame requires, and need not match the wear and losses of a surface handled for centuries. That is where imitation fails.
questions.hint: Ask which features the eye checks before the surface.

questions.topic: Reading a provenance line
questions.learningObjective: Read the order of a provenance line
questions.stem: The log transcribes a provenance line that names a dealer, a country and a collection in that order, and the archivist asks what a reader may take from it.

options.text: That the work is recorded as having passed through a dealer and a named collection, in that order.

options.text: That the work left the country, since a country named in a line is a place of origin.
options.misconception: reads a place of sale as a place of origin

options.text: That the collection is where the work was painted, since a collection gathers what is made nearby.
options.misconception: assumes a collection gathers local work

questions.explanation: A line naming a dealer, a country and a collection records a route, and the order of the entries is the order of the route. It does not show where the work was made.
questions.hint: Read the entries in the order they are given.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Labeling a comparison
questions.learningObjective: Compare two drafts of a comparison label
questions.stem: Two drafts of a comparison label are checked in the log, and the first draft names four features while the second names three of them and adds a phrase about the quality of the handling.

options.text: That the second draft has dropped a feature and added a verdict, and so compares less and ranks more.
That the second draft is the better label, since it is shorter and reads more easily.
options.misconception: assumes shorter is always better

options.text: That the two drafts are both acceptable, since a comparison may describe features or may express an opinion.
options.misconception: treats any comparison wording as acceptable

options.text: That the first draft is wrong, since a label that names four features cannot be a comparison.
options.misconception: assumes a number of features decides the label

questions.explanation: The second draft has given up a feature that could be looked at and taken up a phrase about quality, and a ranking is not a comparison. A shorter label is not a better one.
questions.hint: Ask what the added phrase is doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Deciding about restoration
questions.learningObjective: Explain why inaction is documented
questions.stem: The restoration file in the log records a decision, and the archivist must explain why a decision not to treat a work is also worth writing down.

answer.exemplar: A decision to leave a work alone is a decision, and it is the one most likely to be forgotten, because nothing happened and there is no treatment to point at. Writing down that the panel was examined, that the flaking was judged stable, and that no action was taken protects the object from a later, better informed visitor repeating the whole examination in a hurry, and it records that somebody did look.

questions.explanation: A decision to leave a work alone is still a decision, and it is the one most easily forgotten, since nothing happened. Writing it down stops the same examination being repeated in a hurry.
questions.hint: Ask what a later reader would repeat in a hurry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a forgery has to match
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the features a copy leaves unaddressed
questions.stem: A copy offered for the collection reproduces six of the eight features recorded for the original, and the original's record lists ten features in all. How many of the original's recorded features does the copy not address at all?
questions.explanation: The original's record lists ten features and the copy addresses six, so the features it does not address number ten minus six. That is 4, and the silence is itself evidence.
questions.hint: Subtract the features addressed from those listed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The programme on a church portal
questions.learningObjective: Read the arrangement of a portal

stimulus.body: A log entry describes a church portal where the lintel carries a carved coronation, the left jamb shows figures rising from tombs, and the right jamb shows figures at a table. The entry notes that the jamb scenes face one another and that the coronation is directly above the space between them.

questions.stem: A log entry describes a church portal where the scenes are arranged, and the archivist is asked what the arrangement itself suggests about how the portal was read.

options.text: That the jambs were meant to be read together, since they face one another beneath a scene that joins them.
That the jambs were carved by different masons, since their subjects have nothing in common.
options.misconception: assumes a shared subject means one mason

options.text: That the portal was rebuilt, since medieval masons never placed two different subjects side by side.
options.misconception: assumes the pattern continues forever

options.text: That the coronation was added later, since a central scene is always a later addition.
options.misconception: assumes a central scene is a later addition

questions.explanation: Jamb scenes facing one another beneath a scene placed between them were made to be read together, and the arrangement is part of the argument. It does not show different hands or a rebuild.
questions.hint: Ask why two scenes would face one another.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A charter, a saint, and a gift
questions.learningObjective: Read a charter in two stages
questions.stem: The log asks that a charter be read in two stages: first to state what the document records, and then to state what the reading allows the file to claim.

options.text: State the gift and its terms, then claim only that the shrine held it from that year onward.
State the gift and its terms, then claim that the shrine was founded in the year of the gift.
options.misconception: takes the oldest record as the truest

options.text: State the gift and its terms, then claim that the donor intended the gift to be permanent.
options.misconception: reads a legal document as a statement of intent

options.text: State the gift and its terms, then claim that the object given was made in the same year.
options.misconception: assumes a dated gift dates the object

questions.explanation: The first stage reports the terms of a gift, and the second keeps the claim within them. A charter does not say when a shrine began, what a donor intended for ever, or when an object was made.
questions.hint: State the terms before drawing any conclusion.
